query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, a controlled thermal treatment induces diffusion-driven phase decomposition that causes Mg to segregate preferentially to grain boundaries, forming stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds. These intermetallics then promote the formation of a more protective oxide scale at high temperatures but simultaneously establish localized micro-galvanic cells that accelerate corrosion in aqueous environments compared to the as-cast, metastable state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast alloy featuring a metastable mix of finely distributed solid solutions with some intermetallic precursors, all within a density below 6 g/cm3.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled thermal annealing treatment designed to drive phase transformation (i.e. enhanced diffusion leading to Mg segregation and intermetallic precipitation).
generation.conditions: Samples are compared under identical mechanical and chemical environments: one group remains in the as-cast state, while the other receives the same annealing treatment. Subsequent tests involve high-temperature oxidation in air and corrosion testing in an aqueous electrolyte.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and spatial redistribution (especially at grain boundaries) of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation causes Mg atoms to diffuse and co-segregate at grain boundaries, precipitating as Mg-rich intermetallics. In high-temperature oxidation, these phases facilitate the development of a more adherent, protective oxide scale by acting as nucleation sites or by altering local composition. Under corrosive aqueous conditions, the compositional heterogeneity introduced by these intermetallics gives rise to localized galvanic couples that accelerate corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: After annealing, the alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance (i.e. a thinner, more protective oxide layer) but also show increased susceptibility to corrosion in aqueous environments relative to the initial as-cast state.
generation.baseline: The initial metastable microstructure of the as-cast alloy without a distinct, segregated network of Mg-rich intermetallics.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis specifically applies under conditions typical for high-temperature oxidation (ambient air at elevated temperatures) and electrochemical corrosion in aqueous electrolytes, and for alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3 exhibiting similar compositional complexity.
generation.uncertainty: The precise nature, quantity, and distribution of the Mg-rich intermetallic phases, as well as their detailed influence on corrosion mechanisms, are not fully characterized and may vary with exact alloy composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the given alloy: one kept in the as-cast, metastable state and one subjected to a controlled thermal annealing treatment expected to promote Mg segregation. Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., prolonged exposure to air at a defined elevated temperature) and standardized aqueous corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization in a neutral electrolyte).
measurements: High-temperature oxidation rate (oxide scale thickness and adherence measured via microscopy and weight gain analysis)
Electrochemical corrosion rate (corrosion current density from polarization curves and/or weight loss measurements)
Microstructural characterization (grain boundary analyses via SEM/EDS to detect Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e. a markedly lower oxidation rate or more protective oxide scale) or if they fail to demonstrate an increase in corrosion vulnerability (i.e. similar or lower corrosion rates compared to the as-cast state), then the hypothesis that Mg segregation and intermetallic formation govern the dual behavior is falsified.
